metadata.title: The moderating role of parental support in the relationship between latent profiles of bullying victimization and sense of school belonging: A cross-national comparison

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old students from six regions (five Northeast Asian regions plus the United States) and applies PISA’s two-stage stratified sampling design (schools selected from a national list, then students sampled within schools). The manuscript describes the sampling procedure (including PPS sampling at the school stage) but does not report the specific PISA weight variable(s) used in estimation. For the analytic models, the authors report handling missingness via full information maximum likelihood (FIML) for the latent profile analysis and listwise deletion for key variables in the regression models, but they do not specify whether complex survey weights were applied. Because the paper does not document weight usage, the safest interpretation is that weights were not explicitly incorporated in the reported regression/LPA steps, which may affect population-representativeness and standard errors under PISA’s clustered design.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are composite Likert-scale measures (sense of school belonging and parental support) and bullying victimization indicators used to form latent profiles, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. Missing-data handling is reported as FIML for the latent profile analysis and listwise deletion for key variables in the regression models; therefore, PV-specific missingness strategies are not relevant to this study’s outcomes.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 data for 15-year-old students from five Northeast Asian regions (Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Guangdong China, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan) and the United States. The analytic sample for descriptive statistics and regression models is restricted to cases with no missing values for key variables via listwise deletion (as stated in Table 1 and Table 5 notes). For latent profile analysis, missing values were addressed using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) (Table 3 note). No additional grade restriction is described beyond using students’ reported grade (7–13) as a covariate.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds), bullying victimization profiles vs sense of school belonging (composite Likert)
top_predictors: Victimization profile (selective II vs very low)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multivariate regression (Model 1) coefficients (B, s.e.) reported; no overall ML metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) reported. Example effects: B-S-J-G (China) low profile B=-0.19 (s.e.=0.02, p<.001); medium B=-0.34 (0.03, p<.001); selective B=-0.24 (0.02, p<.001). Hong Kong low B=-0.17 (0.02, p<.001); medium B=-0.30 (0.03, p<.001); selective B=-0.05 (0.02, p<.01). Japan low B=-0.23 (0.03, p<.001); medium B=-0.40 (0.05, p<.001); selective B=-0.14 (0.02, p<.001). South Korea low B=-0.25 (0.04, p<.001); medium B=-0.56 (0.06, p<.001); selective B=-0.28 (0.02, p<.001). Taiwan low B=-0.29 (0.04, p<.001); medium B=-0.50 (0.05, p<.001); selective B=-0.43 (0.04, p<.001). United States low B=-0.29 (0.04, p<.001); medium B=-0.50 (0.05, p<.001); selective B=-0.43 (0.04, p<.001).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged parental interest and latent bullying victimization profile membership to predict students’ sense of school belonging, finding that membership in higher victimization profiles (low, medium, and selective types) was associated with significantly lower belonging compared with the very low victimization profile across all regions. This indicates that anti-bullying interventions should prioritize students experiencing sustained or patterned victimization, because these groups show consistently reduced school connectedness even after adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, and teacher-related covariates.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 (15-year-olds), bullying victimization profiles × parental support predicting sense of school belonging
main_findings.target_variable: Moderation of parental support on the profile–belonging relationship
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multivariate regression (Model 2) interaction coefficients (B, s.e.) reported; no ML metrics. Significant moderation examples: B-S-J-G (China) selective × parental interest B=-0.09 (s.e.=0.04, p<.05); South Korea medium × parental interest B=-0.10 (0.11, not significant) and selective × parental interest B=-0.09 (0.04, p<.05). United States medium × parental interest B=-0.17 (0.07, p<.05) and selective × parental interest B=0.07 (0.06, not significant). Taiwan selective × parental interest was significant and positive (buffering effect described in text), while other regions (Hong Kong and Japan) had largely non-significant interactions.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged parental support (parental interest) and its interactions with latent bullying victimization profiles to predict sense of school belonging, finding that the buffering (protective) moderation of parental support was region-specific—emerging clearly for Taiwan, while interactions were mixed or non-significant in Hong Kong and Japan and sometimes negative in China, South Korea, and the United States. This indicates that family-engagement strategies may need cultural/region-tailored implementation, because parental support does not uniformly buffer bullying-related belonging deficits across all contexts.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-national study used PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old students from five Northeast Asian regions (B-S-J-G China, Hong Kong, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan) and the United States (total N=38,292). Bullying victimization was measured with six offline bullying-frequency items and used to estimate latent victimization profiles via latent profile analysis; sense of school belonging was measured with six Likert items and parental support with four Likert items. Missingness was handled with FIML in the LPA and listwise deletion for key variables in the regression models. The regression results (Model 1) showed that belonging was significantly lower for students in low, medium, and selective victimization profiles versus the very low profile across regions, with coefficients reported in Table 5. Model 2 interaction results indicated that parental support’s buffering role was not consistent across all regions—strongest for Taiwan—highlighting cross-cultural heterogeneity and limiting causal interpretation due to the cross-sectional design.
